text.en: Asha arranged her class books by subject and size. "Elements were arranged in a table in the same way," said her teacher.

Early scientists tried to arrange elements in order. Dobereiner grouped them in triads, and Mendeleev arranged them by atomic mass and left gaps for elements not yet found. He even predicted the properties of germanium, which later matched very closely when it was discovered.
The Modern Periodic Law states that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. In the modern table the elements are arranged in increasing order of atomic number. The horizontal rows are periods and the vertical columns are groups.
The table has s, p, d and f blocks. Group two contains alkaline earth metals. The d block includes the transition elements. The p block contains metals, non-metals and metalloids, while helium is a group eighteen exception with an s-shell configuration. Hydrogen is the lightest and first element of the table.

Group two contains alkaline earth metals. The d block includes the transition elements. The p block contains metals, non-metals and metalloids, while helium is a group eighteen exception with an s-shell configuration.
When two elements show similar reactions, a chemist can compare them as a family. A useful arrangement also lets us see where the similarity stops.
Döbereiner’s lithium, sodium and potassium group is a triad. The properties are similar and sodium’s atomic mass is close to the average of lithium and potassium.
Use approximate masses seven and thirty-nine for lithium and potassium. Half their sum is twenty-three, close to sodium’s atomic mass.
Newlands arranged known elements by increasing atomic mass and noticed a repeating pattern. His law of octaves worked for some lighter elements but did not classify the wider set well.
Mendeleev grouped elements by chemical similarity as well as by atomic mass. He sometimes put a heavier element before a lighter one to keep their chemical families together.
An empty position could be a prediction. Mendeleev proposed properties for an element below silicon. Germanium was later discovered and several comparisons supported the prediction.

board.text: Gap below silicon → prediction about germanium

text.en: Tellurium comes before iodine in the modern table. Although tellurium’s average atomic mass is greater, its atomic number is lower.
Atomic number counts protons. Moseley’s measurements supported arranging the elements by this count. Isotopes of an element then share one position because they share the same proton count.

board.text: Same proton count → same table position

text.en: Read across a period from left to right. Atomic numbers increase one at a time across occupied positions in the full table.
Read down a group to compare a family. The standard long form has eighteen numbered groups and seven periods.
A sodium atom has shell counts two, eight, one. Potassium has two, eight, eight, one. The single outer electron helps explain their similar group one behaviour.

board.text: Na and K each have one outer electron

text.en: Hydrogen is often shown above group one because it has one electron. Its behaviour differs from the alkali metals, so its placement should be read with that distinction in mind.

board.text: Hydrogen is not an alkali metal

text.en: Magnesium and calcium belong to group two, the alkaline earth metals. The simple shell model gives each neutral atom two outer electrons.
Fluorine and chlorine belong to group seventeen, the halogens. Neon and argon belong to group eighteen, the noble gases.
The s, p, d and f blocks relate to subshells being filled in the table. The central block is d. The two rows drawn separately below the table are the f blocks.
The lower f block rows belong to periods six and seven. They are usually drawn separately so the main table can fit across a page.

board.text: Separate display keeps the table compact

text.en: Helium is an important visual exception. Its two electrons occupy the first s subshell, but it sits with the noble gases because its first shell is full.
Metals occupy much of the left and centre. Many non-metals lie toward the upper right. Several elements near the dividing region, such as silicon, are described as metalloids.
A single physical test is not always enough to classify a material. Graphite is made of carbon, a non-metal, and can conduct electricity.
An alloy combines a metal with one or more other elements. Bronze commonly contains copper and tin. The periodic table has entries for those elements, while bronze is a material made from them.

board.text: Bronze: alloy containing copper and tin

text.en: Alloying can change hardness or resistance to corrosion. Two alloys do not necessarily behave the same, because their compositions and structures can differ.
Identify an element from a number and a position. Then state whether the clue described a period, a group or a block, and explain what that clue tells you.
